practice.context: While reading, a student reaches “The biologist observed the nocturnal possum.” They first read “national” for “nocturnal”, then notice the sentence is about animals active at night. What should they do?
practice.correct: Re-read the word, use the letter pattern and sentence meaning, and self-correct to “nocturnal”.
distractors: Keep “national” because it begins with the same letter.
Skip the word and continue without checking meaning.
Replace it with any word that fits the topic.
practice.rationale: Accurate reading integrates grapheme patterns, word parts, grammar and sentence meaning, with self-correction when a first attempt does not fit.
practice.hint: Cross-check how the word looks, sounds, fits grammatically and makes sense.

practice.context: In “The hikers carefully descended the slippery track,” which clue helps a reader predict that “descended” means moved down?
practice.correct: The word part de-/context of hikers and the phrase “the slippery track” together support moving downward.
distractors: The word has the same number of letters as “climbed”.
The sentence contains the word “carefully”.
Any unfamiliar verb can be replaced by “walked”.
practice.rationale: Readers combine word structure and sentence context rather than relying on one clue alone.
practice.hint: Use word parts and the surrounding sentence together.

practice.context: A reader says “The coral reef shelters many species” in a flat rush with no pause at the full stop. Which change improves fluency most?
practice.correct: Read accurately at a meaningful pace and pause at the punctuation so the sentence sounds complete.
distractors: Read as fast as possible.
Pause after every single word.
Change difficult words to easier ones without checking.
practice.rationale: Fluency includes accuracy, appropriate pace and phrasing that reflects grammar and punctuation.
practice.hint: Let punctuation and sentence meaning guide phrasing.

practice.context: A procedure says, “Before attaching the wheels, check that both axles turn freely.” A student reads “after attaching the wheels”. What should alert them to re-read?
practice.correct: The changed word reverses the sequence and conflicts with the procedure’s meaning.
distractors: The sentence is longer than the previous one.
The word “wheels” appears twice on the page.
Procedures never use time words.
practice.rationale: Understanding text structure helps a reader notice when a misread word changes the intended sequence.
practice.hint: Check whether your reading preserves the logical order of the text.

practice.context: A student reads a report about erosion and meets “sediment”. The next sentence says, “These small pieces of rock and soil are carried downstream.” What is the best reading strategy?
practice.correct: Use the explanation in the next sentence to confirm the meaning and then re-read the passage smoothly.
distractors: Guess from the first letter only.
Ignore the word because technical words are optional.
Replace it with “water” because the topic is rivers.
practice.rationale: Topic knowledge and nearby explanations can clarify technical vocabulary and support accurate rereading.
practice.hint: Look for definitions, examples and topic clues around an unfamiliar word.

practice.context: The sentence is “Neither of the puppies was ready to leave.” A reader says “were ready”. What knowledge helps self-correct?
practice.correct: The grammatical pattern “Neither … was” signals that “was” fits the sentence.
distractors: Plural-looking nouns always require “were”.
Meaning never helps with grammar.
The longest verb form is usually correct.
practice.rationale: Grammatical knowledge helps readers predict and verify words that fit the sentence structure.
practice.hint: Ask whether the word fits the sentence’s grammatical pattern as well as its meaning.

test.context: A reader first says “The astronomer inspected the telescope carefully” as “insected”. What is the best correction process?
test.correct: Notice that “insected” does not fit the letters or meaning, re-read the word parts and correct to “inspected”.
distractors: Keep the first attempt to avoid losing fluency.
Skip the word.
Replace it with “looked” without checking the print.
test.rationale: Self-correction uses the printed word and sentence meaning to repair a mismatch.
test.hint: Check print and meaning when a word sounds wrong.

test.context: In a report, “migration” is followed by “the seasonal movement of animals from one region to another.” How should that help a reader?
test.correct: Use the definition to confirm the word’s meaning and read the sentence again with understanding.
distractors: Ignore the definition because it is extra detail.
Change “migration” to “vacation”.
Read only the definition and skip the target word.
test.rationale: Definitions and topic context build semantic knowledge that supports accurate, fluent reading.
test.hint: Use nearby definitions to confirm meaning, then reread in context.

test.context: A sentence ends with a question mark: “Could the storm reach the coast by evening?” Which reading is most fluent?
test.correct: Accurate words, natural phrasing and intonation that signals a question.
distractors: A monotone with no pause.
One-second pauses after every word.
Very fast reading that drops small words.
test.rationale: Fluent reading reflects punctuation and meaning while maintaining accuracy.
test.hint: Let punctuation shape phrasing and expression.

test.context: A set of instructions says, “First fold the card; next draw the window; finally cut along the outside edge.” Why would reading “finally” as “first” require correction?
test.correct: It changes the sequence signalled by the procedure’s structure.
distractors: Both words begin with the same sound.
Instructions do not rely on order.
The sentence would become more imaginative.
test.rationale: Readers use text structure and sequence words to monitor whether a reading makes sense.
test.hint: Use the organisational pattern of the text as a checking cue.
